places.gpt: τοσοῦτον τὴν μουσικὴν ἠξίωσαν θαύματος

judge_A.reasoning: Every witness reads τοσούτου: Bas. 24.7, H 64r.16–17 (το|σούτου), Par. 20v.20–21, V 75v.11–12. No witness has τοσοῦτον, and edition 1 gives no note for it, so it is a slip in that edition. The genitive is also required by the grammar: ἀξιόω takes the person in the accusative (τὴν μουσικήν) and the thing deemed worthy in the genitive (τοσούτου θαύματος). Both editions agree on ἔχον (H Par.) against ἔχων (Bas. V) in the same line, which is right because the subject is τὸ πᾶν.
judge_A.apparatus: None. τοσοῦτον has no witness and is not recorded.

judge_B.reasoning: Bas. 24.7, H 64r.16-17, Par. 20v.20-21 and V 75v.11-12 all read τοσούτου. The construction is ἀξιόω τινά τινος: they 'thought music worthy of so great admiration', with τοσούτου agreeing with θαύματος. Edition 1's τοσοῦτον has no witness and no note to support it. It would leave θαύματος as a bare genitive beside an adverbial 'so much', which is weaker Greek. It looks like a slip of that edition.
judge_B.apparatus: None. There is no variant in the witnesses. If an entry is wanted: τοσούτου Bas. H Par. V (τοσοῦτον, without witness, rejected).

astra.first_view: Print τοσούτου τὴν μουσικὴν ἠξίωσαν θαύματος (reading 2), the reading of Bas., H 64r.16–18, Par. 20v.20–21/21r.1 and V 75v.11–13.
astra.reasoning: I retain the first view; neither edition supplies an argument. Bas., H 64r.16–18, Par. 20v.20–21/21r.1 and V 75v.11–13 all have τοσούτου. The genitive agrees with θαύματος as the complement of ἠξίωσαν: music was deemed worthy of so much admiration. An adverbial accusative is imaginable, but no witness or grammatical necessity supports replacing the unanimous genitive.
astra.apparatus: τοσούτου Bas. H Par. V : τοσοῦτον ed. 1 (without witness support).

terra.first_view: 2: All four witnesses give τοσούτου, a genitive with ἠξίωσαν θαύματος.
terra.reasoning: Bas., H, Par. and V all have τοσούτου; the genitive fits ἠξίωσαν with θαύματος.

reference_check.reasoning: All four witnesses read τοσούτου. LSJ gives the standard acc. + gen. construction of ἀξιόω and a close parallel with a quantity word in agreement (Pl. Lg. 917d). Smyth shows that this kind of hyperbaton is ordinary in prose. Reading 1 is grammatical but has no witness, and nothing makes the transmitted text unacceptable.

places.gpt: εἰ δὲ μὴ οὕτως ἐκφωνηθείη

judge_A.reasoning: H 64v.11, Par. 21r.19 and V 76r.11 all read εἰ γὰρ μή. Bas. stands alone, and its print is actually εἰ δ’ μή, an elided δ’ before a consonant with a clear elision mark (Bas. note; both collators checked the image). That is a typographical anomaly, not a considered reading. Par. prints γάρ with a κ-like compendium sort, the same sort it uses at 21v.18, 25v.15 and 27r.18, where Bas. prints γάρ. A compositor misreading that compendium in the printed copy explains Bas.'s δ’. The sense requires γάρ: the clause gives the reason for the definition just stated by stating its contrary. A note is called ἐναρμόνιος because it can be fitted to another note, for if it is not so uttered it is ἀπηχής and only a ψόφος. δέ would be possible Greek but has no support.
judge_A.apparatus: Positive entry: γὰρ H Par. V] δ’ Bas. (sic, elided before a consonant; = δέ).

judge_B.reasoning: Bas. reads δέ, which per the Bas. note and both collators is actually printed as an elided δ’ before a consonant. Bas. is alone against H 64v.11, Par. 21r.19 (γάρ written with a compendium) and V 76r.11, which all read εἰ γὰρ μή. Explanatory γάρ fits: a note is ἐναρμόνιος because it is so uttered that it can be fitted to another note, 'for if it is not so uttered, it is ἀπηχής'. δέ would also make sense, but an elided δ’ before a consonant looks like a misprint, possibly a misread γάρ compendium in the copy. Edition 1's note agrees, so I made no revision.
judge_B.apparatus: γὰρ H Par. V] δὲ (δ’ ut vid.) Bas.

astra.first_view: Print εἰ γὰρ μὴ οὕτως ἐκφωνηθείη (reading 1), following H 64v.11, Par. 21r.19–20 and V 76r.11 against Bas.'s δέ.
astra.reasoning: I retain the first view. H 64v.11, Par. 21r.19–20 and V 76r.11 have γάρ, naturally introducing an explanation of the preceding definition of ἐναρμόνιος. Bas.'s δέ could introduce a sensible contrast, but is isolated. Edition 1 confirms the useful witness and contextual argument. Its claims concerning an elided δ’, a compendium misprint and translations are not used: the established Bas. line supplied here reads δὲ, and no translations were consulted.
astra.apparatus: γὰρ H Par. V : δὲ Bas.

terra.first_view: 1: H, Par., V give explanatory γάρ, against Bas. δέ.
terra.reasoning: H 64v.11, Par. 21r.19–20 and V 76r.11 have γάρ. The clause explains the preceding definition; Bas. δ’ would also make sense as a contrast, but stands alone.

reference_check.reasoning: The witnesses decide: H, V and Par. read γάρ, and Bas. stands alone. The reference works show that both particles are grammatical and that γάρ/δέ is a known confusion. The familiar idiom εἰ δὲ μή explains how Bas.'s δέ could arise. The explanatory logic suits the author's γάρ.

places.gpt: †ὑπάτη διάτονος†

judge_A.reasoning: All four witnesses read ὑπάτη διάτονος: Bas. 25.6, H 64v.19 (written out in full), Par. 21v.8 and V 76r.21. The position of the note is fixed by its neighbours (παρυπάτη ὑπάτων before it, ὑπάτη μέσων after it), so it is the diatonic lichanos hypaton. The standard name would be λιχανὸς ὑπάτων διάτονος or διάτονος ὑπάτων. The obelus is the wrong tool here, whichever view one takes. If the words are corrupt, the cure (ὑπάτων) is obvious and the sense is certain, so the place is not incurable. If they are the author's, they need no sign. They can be the author's: he uses non-standard names elsewhere, in all witnesses. He writes adjectival διεζευγμένη (τρίτη / διάτονος / νήτη διεζευγμένη) for the standard διεζευγμένων, and παράμεσος for παραμέση. ὑπάτη is itself an adjective in origin, so 'the diatonic of the ὑπάτη tetrachord' is intelligible on the model of διάτονος διεζευγμένη. The form also stands in H, written in full only 32 years after the work was composed. Under the rule 'conjecture only where no witness gives an acceptable text', the unanimous reading is kept without obeli, and the difficulty goes in a note.
judge_A.apparatus: No variant entry. Add a note: 'ὑπάτη διάτονος Bas. H Par. V: the standard name is λιχανὸς ὑπάτων διάτονος / διάτονος ὑπάτων; ὑπάτων διάτονος would be the easy correction (cf. the author's διάτονος ὑπερβολαίων 25.10), but cf. his adjectival διάτονος διεζευγμένη 25.8; not emended.' Edition 2's obeli are an editorial sign, not a reading, and are not recorded.

judge_B.reasoning: Bas. 25.6, H 64v.19 (written in full), Par. 21v.8 and V 76r.21 all read ὑπάτη διάτονος. The standard name of the 4th note is (λιχανὸς) ὑπάτων διάτονος, so the transmitted name is not the theorists' name. The obelus is still the wrong tool. Its position in the list makes clear which note is meant, so the place is not incurable, and the easy cure ὑπάτων would be a conjecture against unanimous witnesses that include H, copied only 32 years after the work was composed. The author's nomenclature is non-standard elsewhere and accepted by both editions: παράμεσος for παραμέση, and the adjectival τρίτη / διάτονος / νήτη διεζευγμένη. After reading the notes, edition 1's point (c) at 25.7 strengthened my view. If the author called the lichanoi 'ὑπάτη διάτονος' and 'μέση διάτονος', then the unanimous μέση μόνως ('plain mese') that follows makes good sense as a contrast, and the lost name would have fallen out by a skip from μέση to μέση. So ὑπάτη διάτονος may well be the author's own form. Print it without obeli and record the expected standard name in the apparatus.
judge_B.apparatus: ὑπάτη διάτονος Bas. H Par. V: the standard name is ὑπάτων διάτονος (λιχανὸς ὑπάτων); ὑπάτων διάτονος could be conjectured (a misread suspended -ων among the surrounding ὑπάτη), but the form may be the author's own (cf. μέση μόνως 25.7). The obeli of the other edition are not adopted.

astra.first_view: Provisionally print ὑπάτη διάτονος without daggers (reading 1): Bas., H 64v.19, Par. 21v.8 and V 76r.21 agree. Flag the unusual note designation in the apparatus.
astra.reasoning: I retain the first view after both arguments. Bas., H 64v.19, Par. 21v.8 and V 76r.21 unanimously name the note ὑπάτη διάτονος. Its position, after παρυπάτη ὑπάτων and before ὑπάτη μέσων, identifies the diatonic member of the lowest tetrachord. Edition 2 rightly stresses the unusual designation, but that does not establish incurable corruption. The nearby adjectival διεζευγμένη and παράμεσος also show that this list is not using a completely regular naming system. I understand this as a nonstandard designation of the lower diatonic note and flag the difficulty in the apparatus. Neither the conjecture ὑπάτων διάτονος nor διάτονος ὑπάτων has witness support. The ancient references cited in the notes were not independently consulted and are not needed for this decision.
astra.apparatus: ὑπάτη διάτονος Bas. H Par. V; ed. 2 obelizes. Note that the sequence points to the diatonic member of the lowest tetrachord; do not attribute a conjectural regularization to a witness.

terra.first_view: 1: All witnesses give ὑπάτη διάτονος; its anomalous note-name need not be treated as incurable.
terra.reasoning: All four witnesses have ὑπάτη διάτονος, despite the position of the note in the sequence. The author also uses nonstandard note names such as διεζευγμένη and παράμεσος; this permits retention without asserting that the words are incurable.
terra.apparatus: ὑπάτων διάτονος and διάτονος ὑπάτων are possible unattested corrections; †ὑπάτη διάτονος† is an alternative editorial judgment.

reference_check.reasoning: Every theorist names this note διάτονος ὑπατῶν / ὑπατῶν διάτονος or λιχανὸς ὑπατῶν. Nicomachus explicitly says the genitive ὑπατῶν is added. ὑπάτη is the name of another note, so the transmitted name is unattested and contradicts itself. The corruption -ων > -η in exactly these names is documented in Cleonides' manuscripts (Jan p. 200). Two things keep the strength moderate. All witnesses agree. And the archetype has the same nominative for genitive plural three times (διεζευγμένη), so archetypal or authorial looseness cannot be fully excluded. The probable original ὑπατῶν διάτονος would be a conjecture, so the obelus is the evidence-based choice between the two readings offered.
reference_check.assessment: Not decisive: the same name ὑπάτη διάτονος stands in the diagram of Theon's codex A (Hiller p. 206, checked on the page image), with διεζευγμένη in the nominative as here; the name is attested, so no obeli.

places.gpt: μέση †μόνος†

judge_A.reasoning: Bas. 25.7, Par. 21v.9 and V 76v.2 all read μόνως, written out. H 64v.20 has only μόν with a curl over the ν at the line end. That is a suspension whose expansion is uncertain: the H notes offer μόν(η), μόν(ος) or μόν(ον), and a curl of this kind can equally stand for -ως. So H does not attest μόνος and cannot be set against the clear reading of the other three. Edition 2 obelizes μόνος, which is one possible expansion of H's compendium, and prints it against three explicit witnesses. That turns an uncertainty in one witness into a corruption of the text. μέση μόνως ('plain mese', 'just mese') makes good sense. It is the only name in the list without a tetrachord qualifier, and comes straight after a run of names ending in …μέσων. Both editions agree on Xylander's supplement ⟨διάτονος μέσων⟩, which the 15-note count of 25.11–17 requires. That is not at issue here. Print: παρυπάτη μέσων, ⟨διάτονος μέσων⟩, μέση μόνως, παράμεσος.
judge_A.apparatus: μόνως Bas. Par. V] μόν(…) H (suspension at the line end, expansion uncertain: μόν(ως)? μόν(ος)? μόν(η)?). Edition 2's †μόνος† is not recorded as a reading.

judge_B.reasoning: Par. 21v.9 and V 76v.2 write μόνως in full, as does Bas. H 64v.20 has only μόν with a curl over the ν at the line end. The H notes leave the expansion open (μόν(η) / μόν(ος) / μόν(ον)), and a sign for -ως cannot be excluded. The witnesses that write the word in full therefore decide, and H is compatible with them. μόνως, an adverb meaning 'solely', gives acceptable sense: 'mese, simply', the one name in this run with no qualifier after a series in μέσων. It makes even better sense if a lost preceding name was 'μέση διάτονος' (see 25.6). Edition 2's μόνος is the least supported expansion of an ambiguous abbreviation. It is also ungrammatical with the feminine μέση, and edition 2 obelizes a reading that no witness clearly has. The wording of the supplement before μέση (⟨διάτονος μέσων⟩ in both editions, Xylander's) is a separate question. If 25.6 is kept as the author's form, ⟨μέση διάτονος⟩ deserves consideration. No revision after reading the notes.
judge_B.apparatus: μόνως Bas. Par. V] μόν + suspension H (μόν(ος)? expansion uncertain)

astra.first_view: Print μέση μόνως (reading 1), as in Bas., Par. 21v.9 and V 76v.1–2. H 64v.20 has the expressly doubtful expansion μέση μόν(ος) [?].
astra.reasoning: I retain the first view. Bas., Par. 21v.9 and V 76v.1–2 expressly give μόνως, which can distinguish 'just mese', without a tetrachord qualifier, from the surrounding qualified names. H 64v.20 has μόν(ος) [?], an explicitly uncertain expansion; the written abbreviation is not secure evidence for the masculine ending. Edition 2's grammatical objection applies to its chosen expansion μόνος, not to the intelligible and amply attested μόνως. An uncertain reading in the oldest witness should not displace the acceptable reading of three others. Xyl.'s separate addition διάτονος μέσων before μέση concerns a missing note in the list, not the validity of μόνως.
astra.apparatus: μόνως Bas. Par. V : μόν(ος) [?] H (abbreviated, doubtful); †μόνος† ed. 2.

terra.first_view: 1: Bas., Par., V give μόνως; H has doubtful μόν(ος). The adverb is defensible as describing μέση named alone.
terra.reasoning: Bas., Par. and V explicitly have μόνως, reasonably meaning that μέση is named without a tetrachord qualifier. H 64v.20 has a suspension whose expansion is uncertain, so it does not compel μόνος.

reference_check.reasoning: The internal arithmetic (15 notes; 1:8 = 8:15) shows a name lost exactly where μόνως stands, and no theorist ever qualifies μέση. Both facts suggest the place is disturbed, which supports marking it. But μόνως is the reading of Bas., Par. and V, and LSJ attests later μόνως = 'simply, only', so 'mese simply' is not impossible. H's μόν(ος) is uncertain, and masculine μόνος with μέση would not agree. The evidence shows a corrupt context more clearly than it shows the word itself is corrupt. The editor may prefer to keep μόνως and mark the lacuna instead.
reference_check.assessment: Weak: the researcher grants that the context (a lost name) is disturbed rather than μόνως itself; his claim that μόνως stands in the place of the lost name was found wrong by the verifier (it follows μέση).

places.claude: ὡς εἶναι τὸ ἡμιτόνιον ὅσον ὀκτὼ ἥμισυ, τὴν δὲ δίεσιν ὅσον ὀκτὼ τέταρτον
places.gpt: ὡς εἶναι τὸ ἡμιτόνιον, οἷον ⟨τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς⟩ ὀκτὼ ἥμισυ, τὴν δὲ δίεσιν ὅσον ⟨τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς⟩ ὀκτὼ τέταρτον

judge_A.reasoning: There are two questions here. (a) οἷον or ὅσον in the first clause. H 65r.16 and V 77r.1 read ὅσον; Bas. and Par. 22r.8 read οἷον. Bas. and Par. both go back to the 1532 princeps, so in effect they are one witness against H, the oldest, and V. In the second clause all witnesses read ὅσον (Bas. 25.25, H 65r.17, Par. 22r.9, V 77r.2). The two clauses are strictly parallel, and ὅσον expresses the quantity the sentence is about. Print ὅσον in both. (b) Xylander's marginal supplement τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς, at both places, is in no witness: H, Par. and V all lack it. It is a conjecture, and the transmitted text does not need it. With the tone set as 9 : 8, ὅσον ὀκτὼ ἥμισυ / ὀκτὼ τέταρτον means 8½ and 8¼, that is, the unit between 8 and 9 halved and quartered. The very next sentence confirms this reading. At 26.1–3 (εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἡ μονὰς οὐ τέμνεται κατὰ τοὺς ἀριθμούς, ἀλλ’ ἡ ἐν ὕλῃ βλεπομένη μονὰς τέμνεται γεωμετρικῶς) the author answers exactly the objection that a unit cannot be split in numbers. That objection only arises if he has just written 8½ and 8¼. Edition 2 also keeps Bas.'s οἷον in the first clause but ὅσον in the second, which mixes the printed and manuscript traditions without any reason. ὀκτωτέταρτον in Bas. Par. against ὀκτὼ τέταρτον in H V is word division only. Print: ὡς εἶναι τὸ ἡμιτόνιον ὅσον ὀκτὼ ἥμισυ, τὴν δὲ δίεσιν ὅσον ὀκτὼ τέταρτον.
judge_A.apparatus: Entry 1: ὅσον H V] οἷον Bas. Par. Entry 2: ὀκτὼ (bis)] τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς ὀκτὼ Xyl. in marg. (utroque loco: «* τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς addo», «† iterum eadem verba addo»). The translator's note should explain the two ways of understanding the passage: 8½ and 8¼ as transmitted, against 'half / a quarter of 9 : 8' with Xylander's supplement.

judge_B.reasoning: There are two questions here. (1) οἷον or ὅσον: H 65r.16 and V 77r.1 read ὅσον ὀκτὼ ἥμισυ, while Bas. and Par. 22r.8 read οἷον. H, the oldest witness, and V give the reading that is parallel to the unanimous ὅσον ὀκτὼ τέταρτον that follows. ὅσον expresses the quantity the passage is about. Bas. and Par. form one print tradition, and they share the one-word ὀκτωτέταρτον. (2) Xylander's marginal τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς, added twice: no witness has these words, so under the edition's rules they are conjectures. They are also unnecessary. The transmitted text means 8½ and 8¼: with the tone at 9:8, the semitone reaches 8½ and the diesis 8¼. The next sentence (26.1-7: the unit is not divided in numbers but is divided in matter, geometrically) justifies exactly this halving and quartering of the unit 9 − 8. Edition 2 both keeps the weaker οἷον and adds an unneeded conjecture. Edition 1's notes argue the same way, so I made no revision.
judge_B.apparatus: ὅσον H V] οἷον Bas. Par. | ὀκτὼ (bis)] τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς ὀκτὼ Xyl. in marg. (conjecture, rejected) | ὀκτὼ τέταρτον H V] ὀκτωτέταρτον Bas. Par. (word division only)

astra.first_view: Print ὡς εἶναι τὸ ἡμιτόνιον ὅσον ὀκτὼ ἥμισυ, τὴν δὲ δίεσιν ὅσον ὀκτὼ τέταρτον (reading 1), following H 65r.16–18 and V 77r.1–2 and declining both of Xyl.'s additions.
astra.reasoning: I retain reading 1 after both arguments, but revise the numerical objection in my initial witness-only reasoning: Xyl.'s added words can be construed with ἥμισυ and τέταρτον as 'half/a quarter of [the ratio] nine to eight', rather than forcing the quotients 9/8.5 and 9/8.25. I therefore do not make that objection decisive. H 65r.16–18 and V 77r.1–2 support ὅσον ... ὅσον; Bas. and Par. have οἷον first. Bas.'s varied wording is possible and H/V could have leveled it, but the oldest witness's quantitative wording coheres with the parallel second clause. All four witnesses lack the supplements. The transmitted eight-and-a-half and eight-and-a-quarter are intelligible as intermediate material magnitudes in the nine-to-eight example, immediately followed by the justification that a material unit can be divided. This does not establish exact mathematical halving of an interval, but neither grammatical understanding nor textual transmission requires Xyl.'s extra words. Preserve the author's formulation and explain its numerical looseness rather than supply an unproved missing phrase.
astra.apparatus: ὅσον H V : οἷον Bas. Par.; ante ὀκτὼ ἥμισυ et ὀκτὼ τέταρτον τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς add. Xyl. in marg. (conjecture); ὀκτωτέταρτον Bas. Par., word division normalized.

terra.first_view: 1: H and V give ὅσον twice; the fractional figures can be read against eight without the unattested double supplement.
terra.reasoning: H 65r.16–18 and V 77r.1–2 have ὅσον in the first clause; Bas. and Par. have οἷον. The second ὅσον is unanimous. The figures 8½ and 8¼ fall between 8 and 9 and can be understood with the author’s following discussion of division, without twice inserting an unattested ratio.
terra.apparatus: οἷον Bas. Par. at first occurrence; τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς added twice Xyl. in margin, conjecture.

reference_check.reasoning: H and V transmit ὅσον ὀκτὼ ἥμισυ … ὅσον ὀκτὼ τέταρτον. LSJ (ἥμισυς II) and Hiller's note on Theon p. 70.6 show that 'numeral + ἥμισυ' without καί is a normal mixed number (8½), and that editors keep it rather than supplement. Theon (pp. 69-70) and Plutarch (De an. procr. 1021e) show that 8½:8 = 17:16 is the arithmetically halved tone. The text's next sentence, on cutting the unit, presupposes exactly these numbers. Xylander's ⟨τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς⟩ is a conjecture in no witness, and the transmitted text is acceptable. ὅσον and οἷον are both lexically fine; ὅσον has the better witnesses (H, V) and parallels the second clause.

places.claude: ἑξκαιδέκατον (26.16), ἑξκαιδέκατος (29.20), and ἑξκαιδέκατον in P fr. 1
places.gpt: ἑκκαιδέκατον (26.16), ἑκκαιδέκατος (29.20), and ἑκκαιδέκατον in P fr. 1

judge_A.reasoning: At 26.16 all four witnesses read ἑξκαιδέκατον: Bas. 26.16, H 65v.13, Par. 22v.6 and V 77v.2. The Bas. note calls it a 'misprint' only by classical standards. The form exists: LSJ has ἑξκαιδέκατος as a lemma of its own ('sixteenth', Hp. Epid. 1.26), Pape gives it for Hippocrates and later writers, and the Greek monolingual dictionary marks it as ancient and medieval. Printing ἑκκαιδέκατον would correct the author's Byzantine usage into classical Greek, which the edition's principles forbid. A ξ/κ difference that changes the form of the word is not a matter of accent or breathing for orthographic normalisation to settle. The author's ἑκκαιδεκάχορδον at 25.12, in all witnesses, is a different word and is kept as it stands: the variation is transmitted and need not be levelled. For P fr. 1 (Vinc. 338.17), P's ἑνδ(έκατον) ('Ms. ἑνδ.') is impossible, because 11 is not a square. The number has to be 16, since its half (8) and its double (32) are not squares, as the text itself says. This P passage is a doublet of 26.13–27.3, so the emendation should take the form of the main text, ἑξκαιδέκατον. That is also closest to Vincent's ἑξδέκατον and to the ἑ-δ letters P reports. At 29.20 I could not see the witnesses, because that line is outside my evidence file. Apply the same rule there: keep ἑξκαιδέκατος if the witnesses agree on it, as edition 1's printing of Bas. implies, and do not normalise it.

judge_A.reasoning: Inside ⟨⟨ ⟩⟩ P is the only witness. Its σύμφρασις (338.4, and ἡ σύμφρασις at 338.7) does not give an acceptable text, so a conjecture is legitimate. LSJ glosses σύμφρασις only as 'continuous speech' (Hdn.Gr., Phot.), which is a term of discourse. Pape and the Greek dictionaries give 'connection of speech' or 'composition of words', never fusion. The argument, however, needs fusion: numbers are immaterial, unmoving and ἄρρευστα and so do not admit X; melodies, being in matter where there is continuity, do admit X; and the length over two strings is joined into one κατὰ συνέχειαν. The fragment opens with εἰ γάρ, so it justifies the preceding main-text phrase ὡς ἓν ἐκ συμφθάρσεως (27.10, unanimous in Bas. H Par. V). LSJ s.v. σύμφθαρσις 2 gives 'melting into one another' (Hermog., Iambl.), and Pape gives 'das Ineinanderfließen und Verschmelzen', exactly the sense required. The contrast with ἄρρευστον ('non-flowing') points the same way. P is shown elsewhere to garble this very word: in fr. 2 it writes ἐξυφθάρσεως twice for ἐκ συμφθάρσεως (Vinc. 340 n. 2), and Vincent himself doubted σύμφρασις (n. 1). The change from σύμφθαρσις to σύμφρασις is easy: θ is lost and αρ/ρα is metathesised, turning a rare word into a familiar one. Vincent's σύγκρασις gives a similar sense, and the Greek Liddell–Scott even glosses σύμφθαρσις by σύγκρασις. But σύγκρασις needs a change of consonants (γκ for μφ) and drops the author's own term. Against the conjecture, P has σύμφρασις consistently, twice, so it is printed as a conjecture with full apparatus. Both editions accept Vincent's accusative τήν at 338.7, and that is not at issue here. Orthography inside the passage is normalised: ἄυλον, ἄρρευστον, διὰ τί.

LSJ gives 'melting into one another' (sense 2) and the joint destruction of components in a mixture (sense 1). Vincent himself distrusted σύμφρασις and suggested σύγκρασις, which is the gloss Liddell–Scott's Greek edition gives for σύμφθαρσις. judge_A.reasoning: The substantive point is βαρεῖ against βάρει. βαρεῖ is the reading of V, and of Bas. with an accent misprint (βαρεί). βάρει is the reading of H (βά|ρει, divided at the line end; the H notes allow it to be βαρεῖ with a misplaced accent) and of Par. The sense needs the adjective, 'the low (note)', set against τοῦ ὀξέος. Compare the same pairing a few lines later: τῶν βαρέων τοῖς ὀξέσιν, ἢ τῶν ὀξέων τοῖς βαρέσι (28.23-24, all witnesses), and τοῦ βαρέος πρὸς τὸ ὀξύτερον (30.2). βάρος ('weight') is not a pitch term; the theorists' abstract noun is βαρύτης. So βάρει is an accent error, shared by H and Par., and not a real variant. ὀξέος against ὀξέως: all four witnesses write ὀξέως. With the article, though, the word can only be the genitive of ὀξύς, not the adverb. The author's own genitive of this adjective type is -έος: τοῦ βαρέος at 30.2, in Bas. H Par. V alike. So -έως here is an ο/ω spelling slip (perhaps under the influence of the ἰσοχρόνως just before), not a Byzantine morphology, and the edition's rule of normalised orthography applies. Edition 1 is wrong in substance because βάρει gives the wrong word. If one preferred to keep the unanimous spelling, the reading to print would be τοῦ ὀξέως τῷ βαρεῖ, which is still not edition 1. A side point I did not decide: H Par. V and Bas. all punctuate after ἀντίφωνον, not after ἰσοχρόνως.

judge_B.reasoning: There are two elements. (1) βαρεῖ / βάρει: V has βαρεῖ. Bas. has βαρεί, a misprint whose accent stands on the ultima, so it agrees with V on the word. H (βά|ρει, divided at the line end) and Par. have βάρει. Sense requires the substantivised adjective: τοῦ ὀξέος τῷ βαρεῖ, 'the high note with the low'. The author pairs the two adjectives in the next lines, τῶν βαρέων τοῖς ὀξέσιν, ἢ τῶν ὀξέων τοῖς βαρέσι (28.23–24, unanimous), and again at 30.2 (τοῦ βαρέος πρὸς τὸ ὀξύτερον). βάρος ('weight') is not used for pitch: the noun for lowness of pitch is βαρύτης. H's accent is a common misplacement in Byzantine accentuation, and the collator's own note reads H's βά|ρει as = βαρεῖ. (2) ὀξέως / ὀξέος: all witnesses have ὀξέως, but with the article τοῦ it can only be the genitive. The author's own genitive of this declension is βαρέος (30.2, Bas. H Par. V), so ὀξέως looks like a scribal ο/ω spelling assimilated to the common adverb. I treat it as orthography to be normalised, not as the author's morphology. If the project prefers to keep ὀξέως as a Byzantine genitive, print τοῦ ὀξέως τῷ βαρεῖ; the substantive decision is βαρεῖ.

judge_A.reasoning: δὶς at 29.8 and 29.9 is in all four witnesses: Bas. (keyed to the margin by *), H 67r.20-21, Par. 24v.2-3 and V 79v.4-6. If δὶς διὰ τεσσάρων is the fourth again in the second octave (28.6-7), then τὸ διὰ πασῶν καὶ δὶς διὰ τεσσάρων means 'the octave plus the second fourth'. That is notes 1 to 8 plus 8 to 11, which gives exactly the δι’ ὀκτὼ καὶ ἡμιτονίου (6 + 2½ tones) stated. Likewise 1 to 8 plus 8 to 12 gives the 9½ tones of δι’ ἐννέα καὶ ἡμιτονίου. A literal 'octave plus two fourths' would be 11 tones and contradicts the author's figures, so the δὶς cannot be a multiplier. It is the author's marker of repetition, unanimous, and also present at 29.14-15 (H V; H Par. V at 29.15) and in P fr. 2. Deleting it classicises the text.

The figures fix the meaning: δι’ ὀκτὼ καὶ ἡμιτονίου (8½ tones = 6 + 2½) and δι’ ἐννέα καὶ ἡμιτονίου (9½ = 6 + 3½). So δὶς is not a multiplier: a literal octave + double fourth would be 11 tones. Preserve the author's intelligible, if redundant, terminology and explain the numerical sense.

terra.first_view: 1: Delete the two unanimous occurrences of δὶς: the given 8½ and 9½ tones require an octave plus a fourth and an octave plus a fifth.
terra.reasoning: Revised after edition 2: the manuscript tradition repeatedly uses δὶς for the fourth or fifth occurring again in the second octave, including P fr. 2 and the lists at 28.6–12. The explicit 8½ and 9½ tones fix the intended compounds. Although deleting δὶς yields standard terminology, the recurrent usage is defensible.
terra.apparatus: δὶς omitted twice by Xyl. in margin, conjectural deletion; retained Bas. H Par. V.

reference_check.reasoning: Unlike place 14, the δὶς here makes the sentence contradict itself: «δι' ὀκτὼ καὶ ἡμιτονίου» and «δι' ἐννέα καὶ ἡμιτονίου» are exactly the octave+fourth and octave+fifth of Cleonides and Gaudentius, under any sense of δὶς. The δὶς is a known volatile element in such names. Against this, the transmission is unanimous, and the intrusion may go back to the author's own conflation with his δὶς-names. So deletion is a conjecture, and the strength is moderate rather than strong.
reference_check.assessment: Not decisive: the researcher's argument that δὶς contradicts the tone counts under any sense fails under the author's own nomenclature (28.6-7), in which δὶς διὰ τεσσάρων is the fourth repeated in the second octave (notes 8-11): octave + that fourth = 1-11 = 8½ tones, as stated. Non-standard but consistent; to be explained in the translator's note.

It is in H 67v.6, Par. 24v.10 and V 79v.13; Bas. alone lacks it. Bas. is inconsistent with itself: it prints δὶς at 29.8-9, where Xylander only proposes deletion in the margin, and drops it at 29.15 against Par. This points to Xylander's own silent regularisation, which at 29.14 happens to agree with an isolated omission in Par. The oldest witness H, with V, has δὶς at both places. That matches the unanimous wording of the same intervals at 29.8-9 and the usage at 28.6-7 and 28.11. The ratios fit the intended octave + fourth and octave + fifth whichever reading is printed: διπλασιεπιμερής 8:3 = 16:6, τριπλάσιος 3:1 = 18:6. Edition 1 here simply prints Xylander's classicised Bas.
judge_A.apparatus: Apparatus: 29.13-14 τοῦ H Par. V] τοῦ δὲ Bas.; 29.14 δὶς H V] om. Bas. Par.; 29.15 δὶς H Par. V] om. Bas. (cf. Xyl. in marg. at 29.8-9). Edition 2's doubt about a possible lost clause ⟨τοῦ δὲ δὶς διὰ πασῶν τετραπλάσιος⟩ is not decided here: keep the text as transmitted, with at most a note.

judge_B.reasoning: There are two elements. (1) δὲ before διὰ πασῶν: only Bas. has it. H 67v.4, Par. 24v.8 and V 79v.11 have τοῦ διὰ πασῶν, and no witness, Bas. included, has δὲ before the next item (29.15). Bas. alone against H Par. V, so delete it. (2) δὶς: H (67v.4, 67v.6) and V (79v.11, 79v.13) have it twice. Par. lacks it in the first item but has it in the second (24v.10 καὶ δὶς διὰ πέντε). Bas. lacks it in both, probably Xylander silently applying his own deletion from 29.8–9, where Bas. still prints δὶς with asterisks. So the archetype, including Par.'s branch, had δὶς here, as at 29.8–9 (unanimous). Par.'s single omission is an isolated slip or normalisation. The ratios (διπλασιεπιμερής = 8:3 = 16:6; τριπλάσιος = 3:1 = 18:6) confirm octave + fourth and octave + fifth, in the author's naming. Medium rather than high confidence because Par. agrees with Bas. in the first item. After reading the notes: edition 2's analysis matches mine. Edition 1 simply prints Bas. without argument. No revision.
judge_B.apparatus: Apparatus: τοῦ διὰ πασῶν H Par. V : τοῦ δὲ διὰ πασῶν Bas. Then καὶ δὶς διὰ τεσσάρων H V : καὶ διὰ τεσσάρων Bas. Par. Then καὶ δὶς διὰ πέντε H Par. V : καὶ διὰ πέντε Bas. (cf. Xyl. ad 29.8–9).

astra.reasoning: Retained the first view after both notes. H 67v.4-6 and V 79v.11-14 retain δὶς at both terms and lack Bas.'s initial δὲ; Par. 24v.8-11 omits δὶς only with the fourth; Bas. omits both. The ratios 16:6 = 8:3 and 18:6 = 3:1 establish octave plus fourth/fifth. As at places 14 and 17, the wording can nevertheless be the author's recurring upper-octave nomenclature rather than literal multiplication. H's priority, its agreement with V, the three-witness agreement at the second δὶς, and the repeated names in section 3 and P outweigh Bas.'s smoother terminology. Edition 2's interpretation of the omissions as regularization is plausible, though deliberate correction by Xylander cannot be proved. H Par. V also support omitting δὲ after the first τοῦ.
astra.apparatus: τοῦ H Par. V : τοῦ δὲ Bas.; δὶς ante διὰ τεσσάρων H V : om. Bas. Par.; δὶς ante διὰ πέντε H Par. V : om. Bas.

The ratios 8:3 and 3:1 identify the octave compounds and do not require removing his δὶς. Bas. omits both; Par. omits the first only. Bas. may reflect correction, but this is an inference.
terra.apparatus: first δὶς omitted Bas. Par.; second δὶς omitted Bas.; Bas. additionally has δὲ after the first τοῦ.

The δὶς is therefore wrong in substance, and Par. lacks it in the first member. But the oldest witnesses (H, V) carry δὶς in both members, and reading 1's δὲ is found in Bas. only. The evidence supports reading 1 on δὶς, while an editor may prefer to drop the unattested δὲ.
reference_check.assessment: Not decisive, for the same reason as 29.8: octave + the second-octave fourth = 1-11 = 8:3 (διπλασιεπιμερής).

places.claude: P fr. 2: πρὸς τὸν προσλαμβανόμενον φθόγγον [conjecture]
places.gpt: P fr. 2: πρὸς τὸν προλαμβανόμενον φθόγγον [as reported]

judge_A.reasoning: Inside the ⟨⟨ ⟩⟩ passage, P as Vincent reports it is the only witness. Vincent prints προ-|λαμβανόμενον (340.9-10) with no footnote, although he records much smaller manuscript readings elsewhere on the page (καθυπ., διαστήματα, κεκρυμμένων). So προλαμβανόμενον is P's reported text. The rules allow conjecture only where no witness gives an acceptable text. προλαμβανόμενον gives a grammatical and tolerable sense: 'the note taken first/beforehand', that is, the base term set first (cf. κείσθω πρῶτος ἐν ἀριθμοῖς ὅρος, 29.17). It also contrasts naturally with the next clause, πρὸς τοὺς πρὸ αὐτῶν ἐγγὺς φθόγγους. Edition 2 itself concedes this 'tolerable sense'. The case for προσλαμβανόμενον is real. It is the standard technical name of note 1 of the Greater Perfect System in every theorist (Cleonides, Bacchius, Aristides Quintilianus, Ptolemy, Nicomachus). The example numbers 6, 8, 9, 12, 16, 18, 24 correspond to notes 1, 4, 5, 8, 11, 12 and 15 counted at 28.19-22. The P scribe also makes many letter-level errors. But both forms name the same note, and the loss of σ cannot be shown to be a corruption rather than a different expression. I could not check the claimed use of προσλαμβανόμενος at 25.4-5 against my evidence files. Print P, and give the conjecture and the technical identification in the apparatus and the translation note.
judge_A.apparatus: Apparatus: προλαμβανόμενον P (Vinc. 340.9-10, sine nota)] προσλαμβανόμενον fort. legendum (coni.; cf. 25.4-5). Translator's note: the note meant is the proslambanomenos, the lowest note of the system = the base term 6 of the example.

judge_B.reasoning: P as reported (Vinc. 340.9–10, printed προ-|λαμβανόμενον with no footnote) reads προλαμβανόμενον. Inside ⟨⟨ ⟩⟩, P is the only witness, and a conjecture is allowed only when it gives no acceptable text. Here it does: 'the note taken first', i.e. the base term (cf. ἀπὸ τοῦ πρώτου φθόγγου, 27.19; κείσθω πρῶτος ἐν ἀριθμοῖς ὅρος, 29.17). It stands in a clear antithesis to the ἄμεσα, which are referred πρὸς τοὺς πρὸ αὐτῶν ἐγγὺς φθόγγους. Later in the fragment the ἔμμεσα are again compared πρὸς τοὺς ἄκρους … τῶν φθόγγων. Vincent was a specialist in Greek music, and he footnoted his corrections elsewhere in the fragment, yet he printed this form without comment. The referent is the same either way: note 1 of the fifteen counted in 28.19–22, i.e. the number 6 of the example. So nothing in the sense requires the change. After reading the notes: edition 2's case for προσλαμβανόμενον is strong. It is the technical name in exactly the same participial shape; the loss of a σ is trivial, possibly at Vincent's line break; and edition 2 reports the term at 25.4–5, which I could not check from my evidence. That case is strong enough for the apparatus but does not meet the rule for printing a conjecture. The P passage may also not be by the author, so the author's usage at 25.4–5 binds it less. Kept, with medium confidence.
judge_B.apparatus: Apparatus: προλαμβανόμενον P (Vinc., without a note, divided προ-|λαμβανόμενον) : προσλαμβανόμενον fort. recte coni. (the technical name of note 1; cf. 25.4–5 if confirmed there). A translation note may name the proslambanomenos.

astra.first_view: Retain πρὸς τὸν προλαμβανόμενον φθόγγον in the double-bracketed P passage (reading 1).
astra.reasoning: Retained the first view despite edition 2's plausible conjecture. Vincent 340.9-10 prints προλαμβανόμενον without a contrary manuscript report. Προσλαμβανόμενος is indeed the name used for note 1 in section 2, and loss of σ would be easy. But προλαμβανόμενον can mean the previously assumed reference note, contrasting the common reference for compound intervals with the immediately preceding notes used for elementary intervals at 340.12. The main text has just established a first numerical term (Bas. 29.17-18). Both readings can refer to the same note, as edition 2 acknowledges. Since the reported text is acceptable, the conjecture belongs in the apparatus rather than the sole-witness P text.
astra.apparatus: προλαμβανόμενον P ut ed. Vincent 340.9-10 : προσλαμβανόμενον ed. 2 (conj.). Entire P passage enclosed in ⟨⟨ ⟩⟩.

terra.first_view: 1: P has προλαμβανόμενον; a previously taken pitch makes sense in the contrast with immediately adjacent notes.
terra.reasoning: P as reported by Vincent has προλαμβανόμενον. It can mean the pitch taken first as the base for the ratios, contrasting with immediately adjacent notes. The author elsewhere uses προσλαμβανόμενος as a technical note name, but the transmitted phrase is intelligible. Print within ⟨⟨the P passage⟩⟩.
terra.apparatus: προσλαμβανόμενον conjecture, attractive as the name of the lowest note.

reference_check.reasoning: προσλαμβανόμενος is the standard technical term (LSJ, Sophocles). The author uses it himself at 25.4-5, and the theorists (Cleonides 5, Gaudentius 16, 20) refer the composite consonances and the system's numbers to that note, as P's sentence does. προλαμβανόμενος has no musical sense or attestation. The variant is a simple loss of σ, with a documented parallel in the προσλαμβάνον/προλαμβάνον confusion in Theon p. 195.
reference_check.assessment: Strong and verified: προλαμβανόμενος is unattested as a note name (LSJ, Sophocles, the theorists); προσλαμβανόμενος is the author's term (25.4-5), and Cleonides Isag. 5 refers the composite consonances ἀπὸ προσλαμβανομένου, as P's sentence does. To the editor.

places.claude: P fr. 2: τὴν ποιὰν τῶν λόγων ἕξιν πεποίηνται
places.gpt: P fr. 2: τὴν ποιὰν τῶν λόγων ἕξιν πεποίηται

judge_A.reasoning: Vincent prints πεποίηνται at 340.13 with no footnote, so this is P's reported reading. πεποίηται has no source: it is a slip in edition 2's transcription of Vincent. The plural verb with a neuter plural subject (τὰ δὲ ἄμεσα) is the usage of the passage itself: τὰ μὲν οὖν ἔμμεσα διαστήματα … ἔχουσι, and τὰ … διαστήματα … κίρνανται in the same period. It is not to be classicised to the singular.
judge_A.apparatus: No entry: πεποίηται has no witness.

judge_B.reasoning: Vincent prints πεποίηνται (340.13) without a footnote, so this is P as reported. Edition 2's πεποίηται is neither P nor Vincent. The plural verb with a neuter plural subject (τὰ δὲ ἄμεσα … πεποίηνται) is the author's own construction in this same sentence: τὰ μὲν οὖν ἔμμεσα διαστήματα … ἔχουσι τὴν ἀναφοράν, and later τὰ … διαστήματα … κίρνανται. Making it singular would be classicising, against the principles. After reading the notes: edition 2 gives no note justifying the change. No revision.

astra.first_view: Retain τὴν ποιὰν τῶν λόγων ἕξιν πεποίηνται (reading 1).
astra.reasoning: Retained the first view; neither edition provides an argument. Vincent 340.13 prints πεποίηνται, with no contrary P footnote. Its subject is τὰ δὲ ἄμεσα καὶ μεταξὺ τούτων κείμενα. The plural verb is acceptable Byzantine agreement, especially since the immediately preceding counterpart τὰ μὲν ... ἔμμεσα διαστήματα takes ἔχουσι at 340.10. Singular πεποίηται would impose a classical agreement rule despite the local usage.
astra.apparatus: πεποίηνται P ut ed. Vincent 340.13 : πεποίηται ed. 2 (conj.).

terra.first_view: 1: P πεποίηνται agrees with plural τὰ ἄμεσα διαστήματα.
terra.reasoning: P as printed by Vincent has plural πεποίηνται, agreeing with τὰ ἄμεσα καὶ μεταξὺ τούτων … διαστήματα. Print within ⟨⟨the P passage⟩⟩.

reference_check.reasoning: Reading 1 is P's own text: Vincent prints it without a 'Ms.' note, although he notes every Ms. difference around it. It is also parallel to ἔχουσι in the same μέν/δέ sentence and to κίρνανται in the next. Jannaris §§1170-1171 shows that a plural verb with a neuter plural subject is normal in post-classical Greek. Smyth §959 shows that even Attic allows it when several items are meant. Reading 2 is a classicising normalisation that no witness has, and the edition's principles exclude it.

places.claude: P fr. 2: τὰ ἐκ συμφθάρσεως διαστημάτων … ὡς ἐκ συμφθάρσεως κίρνανται [conjecture]
places.gpt: P fr. 2: τὰ ἐξ φθάρσεως διαστημάτων … ὡς ἐξ φθάρσεως κίρνανται [Vincent]

judge_A.reasoning: Here both readings are conjectures. The only witness is P, which reads ἐξυφθάρσεως at both places (Vinc. 340 n. 2: 'Ms. ἐξυφθάρσεως … inconnus aux dictionnaires'), and that is not a word, so a conjecture is permitted. Vincent's printed ἐξ φθάρσεως is his own correction. It is ungrammatical (ἐξ before φ) and gives no fitting sense. ἐκ συμφθάρσεως keeps every letter of -υφθάρσεως. It needs only ΕΚ Σ- written as ΕΞ- (κσ = ξ) and the loss of μ before φ. It is also the author's own phrase in the same context, unanimous in Bas. H Par. V: ὡς ἓν ἐκ συμφθάρσεως at 27.10, about exactly the same composite intervals (τριδίεσις, τριημιτόνιον, διτόνιον, τριτόνιον, 27.6-7), and ἓν ἐκ συμφθάρσεως διάστημα at 32.10-11 and ἓν διτόνιον ἐκ συμφθάρσεως at 32.17. The fragment's εἰς ἓν διάστημα ὡς ἐκ συμφθάρσεως κίρνανται almost repeats 27.10. P also garbles the same word in fr. 1 (σύμφρασις).
judge_A.apparatus: Apparatus (at both places): ἐκ συμφθάρσεως coni. (cf. 27.10, 32.10-11, 32.17)] ἐξυφθάρσεως P (Vinc. 340 n. 2) | ἐξ φθάρσεως Vinc.

judge_B.reasoning: P has ἐξυφθάρσεως at both places (Vinc. 340 n. 2, applied to 340.13–14 and 340.18). It is not a word, so P gives no acceptable text and a conjecture is permitted. Vincent's ἐξ φθάρσεως is itself a conjecture, and a bad one: ἐξ cannot stand before φ, and 'from destruction' does not fit κίρνανται / εἰς ἓν διάστημα. ἐκ συμφθάρσεως keeps every transmitted letter of -υφθάρσεως. It needs only the phonetic spelling ἐξ- for ἐκ σ- (κσ = ξ) and the loss of μ before φ. It is also the author's own phrase for exactly these 'incomposite' intervals formed as one: ὡς ἓν ἐκ συμφθάρσεως (27.10; H 66r.12–13 συμφθάρ|σεως), ἓν ἐκ συμφθάρσεως διάστημα (32.10–11) and ἓν διτόνιον ἐκ συμφθάρσεως (32.17), all unanimous. The fragment lists the same intervals as 27.6–7 (τριδίεσις, τριημιτόνιον, διτόνιον, τριτόνιον). After reading the notes: edition 1 makes the same arguments in fuller form. I agree.
judge_B.apparatus: Apparatus, at both places: ἐκ συμφθάρσεως coni. (cf. 27.10, 32.10–11, 32.17) : ἐξυφθάρσεως P (Vinc. n. 2) : ἐξ φθάρσεως Vinc. A cautious alternative for the text would be †ἐξυφθάρσεως†.

astra.first_view: Conjecture ἐκ συμφθάρσεως in both places (reading 1), explicitly distinguishing it from P's reported ἐξυφθάρσεως and Vincent's ἐξ φθάρσεως.
astra.reasoning: Retained the conjecture from the first view. Vincent 340 n. 2 reports ἐξυφθάρσεως at both occurrences; his printed ἐξ φθάρσεως is itself an alteration and leaves ἐξ before a consonant. Edition 1 strengthens the internal argument: ἐκ συμφθάρσεως appears with the same fusion into one interval at Bas. 27.10, 32.10-11 and 32.17; H 69r.14 and 69r.22 confirm the latter two. The recovery of ἐκ σ- behind ἐξ- and a lost μ before φ explains P's reported sequence economically. The context also ends εἰς ἓν διάστημα ... κίρνανται. Edition 2 rightly warns that this cannot establish the exact writing of the unseen manuscript, but printing Vincent's competing conjecture would not solve that limitation. Record P's reported letters faithfully in the apparatus and identify the restoration as conjectural within the double-bracketed P passage. No external lexical citation in the notes is needed for this decision.
astra.apparatus: ἐκ συμφθάρσεως coni. ed. 1 utroque loco, cf. Bas. 27.10 : ἐξυφθάρσεως P teste Vincent 340 n. 2 : ἐξ φθάρσεως Vincent, ed. 2.

terra.first_view: 1: P reports ἐξυφθάρσεως twice; conjecture ἐκ συμφθάρσεως because the author's other usage and the context suggest combination of intervals.
terra.reasoning: P is reported as ἐξυφθάρσεως at both occurrences, not Vincent’s ἐξ φθάρσεως. The former cannot be confidently construed; the author’s repeated ἐκ συμφθάρσεως for the formation of one interval at Bas. 27.10, 32.10–11 and 32.17 makes this conjecture particularly apt. Vincent’s διαστημάτων also replaces P διαστήματα and is needed for the syntax. Both substitutions are marked as conjectural inside the P passage.
terra.apparatus: ἐξυφθάρσεως P (Vinc. 340 n. 2); ἐξ φθάρσεως Vincent; διαστήματα P (340 n. 3), διαστημάτων Vincent.

reference_check.reasoning: The deciding fact is the author's own usage. In every witness he names these very intervals (τριδίεσις, τριημιτόνιον, διτόνιον, τριτόνιον) as one interval «ἐκ συμφθάρσεως» (Bas. 27.10, 32.10, 32.17), and P fr. 2 repeats that list and the «εἰς ἓν» idea. σύμφθαρσις is an established mixture-theory term (LSJ; Alexander, Mixt. 216) and fits κίρνανται. The Ms. ἐξυφθάρσεως is ἐκ συμφθάρσεως with ξ written for κσ and the μ lost. Vincent's ἐξ φθάρσεως breaks the rule for ἐκ before consonants (Smyth §136). It also rests on a word attested only marginally (Bailly) and gives weaker sense.

places.claude: P fr. 2: τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς κεκρυμμένων διαστημάτων
places.gpt: P fr. 2: τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς κεκραμένων διαστημάτων

judge_A.reasoning: P reads κεκρυμμένων (Vinc. 340 n. 4: 'Ms. κεκρυμμένων'). κεκραμένων is Vincent's correction, which under the rules is a conjecture, and P's text needs none. 'The intervals hidden (latent) within them, whose ratios were set beforehand against the adjacent notes' gives exact sense. It matches the author's account of incomposite intervals: δύναμιν μὲν ἔχον διαφόρων διαστημάτων, δι’ ἑνὸς δὲ διαστήματος ἀπηχούμενον (27.12-14). The component intervals are present in potency but not heard. Vincent's κεκραμένων would anticipate the sentence's own κίρνανται, producing the near-tautology 'the intervals mixed in them … are mixed into one interval'. The best support for Vincent is the author's συγκεκραμένον at 32.12, which deserves mention in the apparatus. It does not make P's reading unacceptable.
judge_A.apparatus: Apparatus: κεκρυμμένων P] κεκραμένων Vinc. (cf. συγκεκραμένον 32.12).

judge_B.reasoning: Vinc. 340 n. 4 reports 'Ms. κεκρυμμένων'. Vincent's κεκραμένων is a conjecture. P's reading gives good sense, so it must be kept: τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς κεκρυμμένων διαστημάτων means 'the intervals hidden, latent, in them' (in the tridiesis, trihemitone, ditone, tritone). This is exactly the doctrine of the main text: such an interval is δύναμιν μὲν ἔχον διαφόρων διαστημάτων, δι’ ἑνὸς δὲ διαστήματος ἀπηχούμενον (27.12–14). In the genitive absolute, the component intervals were assigned their ratios beforehand and lie hidden in the single interval, which then sounds as one. Vincent's form was prompted by κίρνανται at the end of the sentence. The author's συγκεκραμένον (32.12) lends it some colour, but that same echo makes κεκραμένων the easier reading, and a scribe would more likely have produced it than κεκρυμμένων. After reading the notes: edition 2 argues the same. Edition 1 has no note. No revision.
judge_B.apparatus: Apparatus: κεκρυμμένων P : κεκραμένων Vinc. (cf. κίρνανται and 32.12 συγκεκραμένον).

astra.first_view: Retain τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς κεκρυμμένων διαστημάτων (reading 2).
astra.reasoning: Retained the first view. Vincent 340 n. 4 explicitly reports Ms. κεκρυμμένων; κεκραμένων is his printed correction. Edition 1 rightly observes that 'blended' echoes the final κίρνανται. Nevertheless, the constituent intervals can intelligibly be 'hidden' or latent within the larger interval; their ratios are first considered separately and they are then combined into one. The original reading is therefore acceptable, as edition 2 argues, and an attractive echo does not justify replacing the only reported manuscript reading.
astra.apparatus: κεκρυμμένων P teste Vincent 340 n. 4 : κεκραμένων Vincent, ed. 1 (conj.).

terra.first_view: 2: P has κεκρυμμένων; constituent intervals may be described as hidden in the larger interval, so preserve the witness provisionally.

judge_A.reasoning: H 69r.19 reads γοερώτερο(ν); Bas. 32.15, Par. 26v.11 and V 82r.1 read γοέτερον. γοέτερον is not a Byzantine variant of the comparative. It has lost part of the stem (γοε[ρω]τερον), and no adjective yields such a form; even a levelled Byzantine comparative would be γοερότερος. The regular comparative of γοερός is γοερώτερος, and the sense demands a comparative of 'mournful' alongside παθητικώτερον. Xylander's own Latin, 'ad … luctum ciendum efficacius', renders exactly that. This is a shared error of the branch Par. V Bas., and the oldest witness keeps the correct form. The edition's principle of correcting Bas. by the oldest manuscript applies. Edition 2's objection that it would be 'classicising' does not hold, because there is no Byzantine form to protect.

judge_B.reasoning: H 69r.19 has γοερώτερο(ν). Bas., Par. 26v.11 and V 82r.1 have γοέτερον. γοέτερον is no Greek form: there is no positive from which it could be formed. It is not Byzantine usage but a mechanical loss of the syllable -ρω- (γοε[ρώ]τερον), perhaps helped by the familiar ending -έτερος. The comparative of γοερός (short syllable before the ending) is regularly γοερώτερος. This is the case where the oldest manuscript corrects the shared error of the printed tradition and its relative V. It is also paired with παθητικώτερον, as the sense requires. Xylander's version ('ad … luctum ciendum efficacius') presupposes the comparative of γοερός. After reading the notes: edition 2 doubts the change in order not to 'classicise the author's possible usage', but an impossible form is not usage. Not convinced; no revision.

astra.reasoning: Retain my first view after reading both arguments. H 69r.19 has γοερώτερο(ν), while Bas. 32.15, Par. 26v.11 and V 82r.1 give γοέτερον. The regular comparative of γοερός fits the description of the chromatic genus beside παθητικώτερον. Edition 2 rightly cautions against classical normalization, but this is a choice between transmitted readings, and no comparable formation elsewhere in the supplied text supports the shortened adjective. Loss of ρω offers a plausible explanation of the shorter reading. Edition 1 strengthens the morphological case, but its absolute claim that γοέτερον cannot be Greek and its proposed genealogy go beyond what the supplied evidence proves. H may itself have regularized the word, so confidence remains medium.

|23.1|Τῆς μουσικῆς |23.2|σύνοψις ἠκριβωμένη

|23.3|Μουσικὴν οἱ παλαιοὶ συνέ|23.4|χειν εἶπον τὸ πᾶν· οὐδὲν |23.5|γὰρ τῶν ὄντων συμμετρί|23.6|ας ἄτερ καὶ ἀναλογίας ἐστίν. |23.7|ἀλλ’ οὐδέ τι τῶν γινομένων, |23.8|μὴ μετὰ συμμετρίας τῆς προσηκούσης καὶ |23.9|ἀναλογίας γινόμενον, καλῶς ἄν ποτε γένοι|23.10|το, κἂν τεχνητὸν εἴη, κἂν φυσικόν, κἂν αἰσθή|23.11|σει ληπτόν, κἂν περὶ μόνην νόησιν θεωρούμενον. |24.1|ἡ δὲ μουσικὴ αὐτοσυμμετρία τίς ἐστι καὶ |24.2|ἀναλογία, τὸ πᾶν, οἷα τοῦ παντὸς ἁρμονία |24.3|τυγχάνουσα. τάχα δ’ ἄν τις καὶ τὸ θεῖον αὐ|24.4|τὸ οὐκ ἀπεικότως ἁρμονίαν ἑαυτοῦ τε καὶ τοῦ |24.5|παντὸς ὀνομάσοι, ἐν ᾧ τὸ πᾶν συναρμολο|24.6|γούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον εὖ τε καὶ ὡς |24.7|ἄριστα διαφαίνεται ἔχον. τοσούτου τὴν μου|24.8|σικὴν ἠξίωσαν θαύματος. ἧς ἐν ἅπασιν οὕ|24.9|τω θεωρουμένης καὶ πάντα διεπούσης καὶ |24.10|κοσμούσης, καὶ ἡδονὴν μὲν τῇ αἰσθήσει, ἁρ|24.11|μονίαν δὲ τῇ φύσει, μακαριότητα δὲ τῇ νοή|24.12|σει χαριζομένης, περὶ τῆς ἐν αἰσθήσει μουσικῆς, |24.13|μᾶλλον δὲ τῆς ἐν μιᾷ τῶν αἰσθήσεων τῇ ἀκοῇ |24.14|θεωρουμένης, ἐν ἐπιτόμῳ διαληψόμεθα.

|24.15|Φθόγγος ἐστὶ φωνῆς ἀδιαστάτου ἐναρμό|24.16|νιος τάσις. διάστημα δὲ φθόγγων ἡ πρὸς |24.17|ἀλλήλους ποιὰ σχέσις. σύστημα δὲ ποιὰ |24.18|διαστημάτων περιοχή. ἁρμονία δὲ συστη|24.19|μάτων σύνταξις.

Ὁ μὲν οὖν φθόγγος ἀδιά|24.20|στατός ἐστιν, ὡς ἡ ἐν γεωμετρίᾳ στιγμή· ἐναρ|24.21|μόνιος δὲ λέγεται διὰ τὸ οὕτως ἐκπεφωνῆ|24.22|σθαι ὡς δύνασθαι καὶ μεθ’ ἑτέρου φθόγγου ἐναρμο|24.23|σθῆναι. εἰ γὰρ μὴ οὕτως ἐκφωνηθείη, ἀπηχής |24.24|ἐστι φθόγγος, οὐκ ἐναρμόνιος· οὐδ’ ἂν φθόγγος |24.25|ὅλως καλοῖτο, ἀλλὰ ψόφος τις ἄλλως ἐκπε|25.1|φωνημένος καὶ πρὸς ἁρμονίαν οὐκ εὔχρη|25.2|στος.
